brief_summary: The ASSIST trial evaluates whether an AI-assisted smartphone application can reduce post-traumatic stress symptoms and other psychological distress in family members of critically ill patients. Admission to an intensive care unit (ICU) places a severe psychological burden on families, often leading to post-intensive care syndrome-family (PICS-F). Current support is mostly reactive and rarely available after the patient is discharged. This study is a three-center randomized controlled trial involving 1000 family members. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive either standard care or standard care plus the ASSIST smartphone platform. During the ICU stay, the platform uses an artificial intelligence model to simplify clinical information (approved by a clinician) and helps families prepare questions for the medical team. After the patient is discharged, the platform monitors the family member's mood daily. If a risk of anxiety or depression is detected, it provides a brief digital cognitive behavioral therapy module. The main goal is to see if the ASSIST platform reduces post-traumatic stress over a 12-month period compared to standard care alone. Secondary goals include evaluating its effects on acute stress, decisional conflict, anxiety, depression, and caregiver burden. The study will also include qualitative interviews to understand the family members' lived experiences using the platform
title: AI-Assisted Adaptive Support to Reduce Post-Intensive Care Syndrome-Family

brief_summary: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a highly prevalent condition that incurs an economic burden in excess of $232 billion annually in the United States alone. Demand for trauma-focused treatment has consistently increased in recent decades. Written Exposure Therapy (WET) has emerged as a gold-standard treatment for PTSD in the most recent clinical practice guidelines. The relatively shorter protocol for WET may make it a more efficient and cost-effective option in certain settings when compared to longer trauma-focused therapies. There have been limited efforts to develop and validate a protocol that adapts WET to be delivered in groups. Group therapies have been recognized as cost-effective, feasible, and efficacious approaches to treating conditions while increasing access to care. Our objective is to employ a between groups, repeated measures randomized controlled design to test whether WET adapted to and delivered in a group format is noninferior to individually delivered Written Exposure Therapy in changing symptoms (e.g., PTSD, depression, anxiety, insomnia; Aim 1) among active duty Servicemembers. We also aim to examine and compare implementation related outcomes, including treatment feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, and costs (Aim 2). We hypothesize that 1) WET delivered in a group format will be noninferior to WET delivered individually on measures of PTSD, depression, anxiety, and insomnia; 2a) There will be no differences between treatment conditions on measures of feasibility, acceptability, and fidelity; and 2b) Treatment cost will be significantly lower for the Group WET condition when compared to the cost of Individual WET. We envision that this knowledge will help inform clinical guidelines and improve access and availability to gold-standard evidence-based trauma focused psychotherapies.
title: Comparing Individual Versus Group Written Exposure Therapy Among Active Duty Servicemembers

brief_summary:
1. Background and Rationale Problem: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of global and national mortality (accounting for 15.9% of deaths from ischemic heart disease in Colombia in 2019). Prolonged bed rest and extended stays in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) lead to severe physical deconditioning and multisystem deterioration.
2. Knowledge Gap: Although High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) has proven effective and safe in outpatient cardiac rehabilitation settings (Phase II), there is a significant lack of evidence regarding its early application in critically ill postoperative patients directly within the ICU (Phase I).
3. Main Objective To evaluate the feasibility, safety, and tolerance of implementing an adapted interval cardiovascular rehabilitation protocol in postoperative coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) patients during their ICU stay.
4. Methodology and Study Design Study Design: Prospective, single-arm, intrahospital feasibility pilot study.
5. Population and Sample: 15 adult patients following coronary artery bypass graft surgery admitted to the ICU at Clínica Imbanaco S.A.S.
6. Main Inclusion Criteria: Ejection fraction \>40%, hemodynamic and respiratory stability, extubation with spontaneous stable breathing, cooperative alert level (RASS between -1 and +1), and medical clearance.
7. Intervention (Adapted HIIT Protocol) Device: Lower-limb cycle ergometer adapted in a seated position.

   Session Structure (Total duration: 18 ± 2 minutes):

   Warm-up (5 min): Global joint mobilization and education on diaphragmatic breathing patterns.

   Main Phase (HIIT) (8 min): 6 interval cycles consisting of 30 seconds of high-intensity pedaling (guided by the Borg CR-10 scale with a threshold ≥6/10) alternated with 1 minute of rest.

   Cool-down (5 min): Gentle movements and controlled deep breathing.
8. Monitoring: Continuous tracking of heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ), and perceived exertion (Borg scale).
9. Variables and Outcomes Feasibility: Screening rates, eligibility, recruitment, adherence, protocol completion, and data completeness.

9.1.Safety: Recording of adverse events (cardiovascular, respiratory, arrhythmias, or post-exercise hypotension).

9.2Tolerance: Borg scale, visual analog scale (VAS) for pain, and clinical signs of fatigue or dyspnea.

9.3Functional Capacity \& Recovery: 6-minute walk test (6MWT), muscle strength (MRC scale), functional independence (Barthel Index), ICU length of stay, and total hospital length of stay.
primary_outcomes: Safety and Adverse Events Incident Rate
Hemodynamic and Physiological Response During Rehabilitation Protocol
Subjective Effort Tolerance via Borg Scale
Subjective Pain Evaluation via Visual Analog Scale
title: Feasibility, Safety and Tolerance of Interval Cardiac Rehabilitation in ICU After Coronary Artery Bypass Surgery

brief_summary: This study is designed as a prospective, parallel three-arm (1:1:1 allocation ratio), dose-controlled, assessor- and analyst-blinded, superiority randomized controlled clinical trial. Sixty-six patients aged 40-75 years who have undergone CABG, are referred to the Phase II cardiac rehabilitation unit, meet the eligibility criteria, and provide written informed consent will be randomly allocated into three groups (n = 22 per group) using computer-based adaptive Urn randomization. All three groups will undergo a 6-week intervention (4 days/week, 24 sessions in total) standardized to an isocaloric weekly workload of \~540 MET-minutes/week (135 MET-minutes/session) in accordance with the American Society for Preventive Cardiology (ASPC) guidelines: (1) Standard Continuous Aerobic Exercise Group (45 minutes of continuous cycle ergometer training per session at 30-40% of maximal heart rate \[HRmax\], 3 METs, \~50 Watts); (2) Accumulated-Fractionalized Aerobic Exercise Group (3 bouts of 8 minutes of cycle ergometer training per day \[total 24 minutes/day\] separated by at least 30 minutes of passive rest between bouts, at 60% HRmax, 5.5 METs, \~100 Watts); and (3) Lower-Extremity Functional Exercise Group (a 12-cycle protocol combining the 30-Second Sit-to-Stand and 2-Minute Step exercises with a 1:1 work-to-rest ratio, totaling 30 minutes of net active exercise per session at 4.5 METs, HRmax \<=60%, Borg RPE 11-13). Primary outcome measures are changes from baseline in functional mobility assessed via the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test and submaximal exercise capacity assessed via the 6-Minute Walk Test (6-MWT) distance at Week 6. Secondary outcomes include routine transthoracic echocardiographic parameters (left ventricular ejection fraction \[LVEF\]) and hemodynamic responses (heart rate, blood pressure, peripheral oxygen saturation \[SpO2\], and Borg dyspnea/fatigue ratings).
primary_outcomes: Change from Baseline in Timed Up and Go (TUG) Test Completion Time at Week 6

A total of 99 first-year nursing students at a public university in Türkiye were randomly assigned to either a flipped learning group (n = 54) or a traditional lecture-based teaching group (n = 45).

Students in the flipped learning group received interactive educational videos and learning materials before class and participated in mind mapping, role-play activities, and error-focused feedback during the classroom session. Students in the control group received traditional lecture-based instruction. Both groups received the same content on body temperature, pulse, respiration, and blood pressure measurement.

Students' knowledge was assessed before and after the intervention, while measurement skills and learning motivation were evaluated after the intervention using assessment checklists and a motivation questionnaire.

In addition, interviews and learning diaries were used to explore students' experiences with flipped learning.

The study examined whether flipped learning could improve nursing students' knowledge, practical measurement skills, and motivation compared with traditional teaching.

brief_summary:
Background: Thalidomide is a medication that was prescribed in the late 1950s and early 1960s, including for morning sickness in pregnancy. It was later found to cause serious birth defects if taken during early pregnancy. People born with these effects are often referred to as "Thalidomide survivors" or people with thalidomide embryopathy. Many have limb differences (such as shortened or missing arms or legs), hearing or facial differences, or internal organ involvement. The majority of Thalidomide survivors live with long-term muscle and joint pain, which can have a major impact on daily life, wellbeing, and independence. Although pain services exist, survivors often find that current support does not fully meet their complex and individual needs. Through an earlier project called TRIUMPH-TS, Thalidomide survivors, clinicians, and researchers worked together to design a new, tailored pain management pathway specifically for this community.

Aim: The COMPASS-TS study aims to test how well this new pain management pathway works in real life. The study will explore whether the pathway is helpful and acceptable for Thalidomide survivors, and whether it can be delivered effectively by clinicians in routine practice. It will also help identify what works well and what could be improved.

Methods: Thalidomide survivors with long-term pain, as well as the clinicians involved in delivering the pain management pathway, are invited to take part. Survivors will be randomly allocated either to follow the new pathway or to continue with their usual care. Everyone will be asked to complete questionnaires about how pain affects their life. Some participants will also take part in interviews to share their experiences. Survivors who initially continue with usual care will later be offered the new pathway as well. The new pain management pathway brings together a specialist team, including physiotherapists, pain doctors, nurses, pharmacists, and the Thalidomide Trust's medical advisor. Together with each survivor, they create a personalised plan that may include advice on medicines, gentle exercise, activity pacing, sleep support, relaxation techniques, and wellbeing advice.

Impact: The findings from COMPASS-TS will help improve future pain services for Thalidomide survivors and others living with long-term pain.
primary_outcomes: Acceptability of the COMPASS-TS Community Pain Management Pathway
title: Community Pain Management Service for Thalidomide Survivors

brief_summary:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a long-term respiratory condition that can cause breathlessness, fatigue, and difficulties performing daily activities. Pulmonary rehabilitation, which combines exercise training and education, can help people with COPD improve their symptoms and quality of life. However, access to pulmonary rehabilitation programs remains limited, particularly in primary healthcare settings.

This randomized controlled trial aims to evaluate the effects of a 12-week pulmonary rehabilitation program delivered in primary healthcare facilities in São Carlos, Brazil, on health status in people with COPD.

Approximately 40 participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups: a pulmonary rehabilitation group or a usual care group. Participants in the rehabilitation group will attend two supervised sessions per week, including aerobic and resistance exercises, health education, and strategies to support behavior change. Participants in the control group will continue receiving usual care.

The main outcome will be the change in health status from baseline to the end of the 12-week program. Additional assessments will examine physical function, symptoms, daily activities, quality of life, and voice-based acoustic biomarkers. Changes in voice characteristics will also be explored to investigate their potential as indicators of responses to pulmonary rehabilitation. Follow-up assessments will be conducted three and six months after the rehabilitation program.

brief_summary:
This study aims to investigate how different methods of producing pea protein ingredients influence amino acid levels in the blood after consumption. Pea protein ingredients produced by dry and wet fractionation differ in their composition and physical properties, which may affect how proteins are digested and how amino acids appear in the bloodstream.

In this pilot study, 18 healthy adults aged 18-55 years will consume four pea protein beverages on separate occasions. The beverages will contain a dry-fractionated pea protein concentrate (Dry-P), two recombined ingredients prepared using wet-fractionated pea protein isolates (Wet-P1 and Wet-P2), and a heat-treated version of the dry-fractionated concentrate (Dry-Pheated). Each beverage will provide 20 g of protein. The main objective is to compare the total amino acid response in the blood over five hours after consumption of Dry-P and Wet-P1. Additional comparisons will investigate differences between the two wet-fractionated protein formulations and the effect of heat treatment on the dry-fractionated concentrate. Changes in blood glucose and insulin levels will also be explored.

The study will help improve understanding of how pea protein processing influences postprandial amino acid responses in humans.

Wet-P2: Recombined wet-fractionated pea protein ingredient (supplier 2)

primary_outcomes: Incremental area under the curve (iAUC) of plasma total amino acid (TAA) concentrations

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to evaluate the effectiveness of psychoeducation on sleep hygiene in reducing insomnia symptoms among young adults aged 18-26 years with mild to severe insomnia symptoms in Malaysia. The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Does structured psychoeducation on sleep hygiene improve sleep hygiene behaviours among young adults, as measured by the Sleep Hygiene Index (SHI)?
* Does structured psychoeducation on sleep hygiene reduce insomnia symptoms among young adults, as measured by the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI)?

Researchers will compare participants receiving a structured three-session psychoeducational intervention with those receiving general printed sleep education materials (active control group) to determine whether the structured intervention leads to greater improvements in sleep hygiene behaviours and reductions in insomnia symptoms.

Participants will:

* Complete an initial screening to determine their eligibility for the study.
* Provide informed consent and complete baseline assessments, including the Sleep Hygiene Index (SHI) and Insomnia Severity Index (ISI).
* Be randomly assigned to either the treatment group or active control group in a 1:1 ratio.
* Treatment group: Attend three psychoeducational sessions on Days 1, 7, and 14, covering an introduction to sleep, sleep efficiency, and sleep hygiene behaviours, based on the Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) treatment manual.
* Active control group: Receive printed psychoeducational materials containing general information and facts about sleep on Days 1, 7, and 14, without structured behavioural exercises.
* Complete post-intervention assessments using the SHI and ISI following the third session to evaluate changes in sleep hygiene behaviours and insomnia symptoms.
title: Effectiveness of Sleep Hygiene Psychoeducation in Reducing Insomnia Symptoms

brief_summary:
Heart valve disease-severe narrowing (stenosis) or leaking (regurgitation) of a heart valve-is often treated with surgery to replace the diseased valve. Current artificial valves have important limitations: mechanical valves require lifelong blood-thinning medication (anticoagulation), which carries a risk of bleeding and complicates daily life; conventional biological valves gradually wear out and calcify, particularly in children and young patients, who may outgrow their prosthesis and face repeated reoperations throughout life. This is known as prosthesis-patient mismatch.

This study evaluates a new type of biological heart valve, the Novel Cellularized Heart Valve (NCHV). The NCHV is a biological valve prepared from specially treated natural valve tissue that preserves the native valve architecture and hemodynamic performance. The key design concept of the NCHV is its capacity for in vivo cellularization: after implantation, the patient's own cells are expected to migrate into the valve tissue and repopulate it, accompanied by gradual matrix remodeling. This biological regeneration process is intended to make the valve more durable, more resistant to calcification and structural deterioration, and potentially able to grow with the patient-thereby reducing the need for repeated reoperations. Because it is a biological valve, recipients are also expected to avoid lifelong anticoagulation, unlike patients with mechanical valves.

This is a prospective, exploratory study conducted at Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, China). Approximately 30 patients with severe aortic or pulmonary valve stenosis or regurgitation-including patients with congenital heart disease, infective endocarditis, or a previously implanted valve that has failed-will receive an NCHV during planned heart surgery. The valve comes in six sizes (17-27 mm) to fit different patients.

After surgery, participants will be followed at 1 week, 1, 3, 6, and 12 months with heart ultrasound (echocardiography), blood tests, and clinical examination. Long-term follow-up with ultrasound and chest X-ray will continue annually up to 5 years. The main purpose is to assess whether the valve still works properly 12 months after implantation. Safety will be monitored throughout, recording any device- or surgery-related problems such as valve leakage, blood clots, infection, or the need for reoperation.

The study is sponsored by Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology. Participants will receive the study valve, related examinations, and clinical follow-up free of charge, and the sponsor has purchased clinical trial insurance for all participants.
lead_sponsor: Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology
title: A Prospective Study of a Novel Cellularized Heart Valve for Heart Valve Disease

brief_summary:
Open liver surgery presents perioperative management challenges compared to other types of open abdominal surgery. Specifically, postoperative coagulopathy-resulting from hepatic impairment-and the use of a "low central venous pressure" (CVP) strategy are both at odds with the use of epidural anesthesia. This is due to the risks of spinal hematoma (associated with the removal of the epidural catheter) and prolonged hypotension (caused by the sympatholysis induced by the epidural).

Furthermore, the available pharmacological options are limited; there is a risk of local anesthetic toxicity if these agents are administered intravenously (due to the hepatic metabolism of lidocaine), as well as a risk of paracetamol toxicity should hepatic impairment occur.

Current clinical practice is guided by several consensus statements:

* The 2023 ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) guidelines advise against the routine use of epidural anesthesia, citing the aforementioned risks, and instead encourage the use of alternatives such as abdominal wall blocks or intrathecal morphine.
* The 2021 PROSPECT guidelines suggest a multimodal approach combining paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) with either a thoracic epidural or bilateral subcostal oblique abdominal wall blocks.

It should be noted that while the French Society of Anesthesia and Intensive Care Medicine (SFAR) has not issued specific guidelines for liver surgery, their 2016 recommendations on postoperative pain management suggest the placement of a wound catheter for continuous local anesthetic infusion in cases of laparotomy where neuraxial analgesia is not employed. In light of these factors, locoregional analgesia appears essential, though the role of epidural analgesia remains a subject of debate. Furthermore, it is evident that certain locoregional analgesia techniques-such as the paravertebral block-have not been extensively studied or compared.

The objective of this study is therefore to assess current practices within our department and compare them against existing clinical guidelines. This work could serve as a foundation for developing future departmental protocols and implementing prospective studies that compare emerging locoregional analgesia techniques.
primary_outcomes: Prevalence of locoregional anesthesia in major or minor hepatic surgery performed via a subcostal laparotomy
title: Locoregional Anesthesia in Hepatic Surgery Via Subcostal Laparotomy: a Retrospective Study

brief_summary: The study will use a randomized controlled trial design conducted over ten months at Special Needs and Autism Centre and Little Angels, Sialkot. It will include 26 children aged 8-12 years with Autism Spectrum Disorder, randomly allocated into an adapted rhythmic gymnastics group and a regular physical activity group. Motor skills and repetitive behaviour will be assessed using the Test of Gross Motor Development (TGMD) and Repetitive Behavior Questionnaire-3 (RBQ-3), respectively. Ethical approval will be obtained from the Research Ethical Committee of Riphah International University, Lahore, and data will be analyzed using SPSS version 23.0.
primary_outcomes: Test of Gross Motor Development-2nd Edition (TGMD2)
title: Effects of Gymnastics on Motor Skills

Participants received a single 60 mg subcutaneous injection, two 45 mg injections one week apart, or matching placebo at the start of the menstrual cycle, and were monitored until Day 29 and then until menses returned.
primary_outcomes: TmaxInit2 (2 × 45 mg arm only). Times are relative to the first dose
title: Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics and Safety of a Long-Acting Teverelix Depot in Healthy Female Volunteers

primary_outcomes: Time to first event of any component of MACE-PLUS

brief_summary:
The goal of this study is to learn whether video-assisted self-assessment with structured feedback improves nurses' peripheral intravenous catheter (PIVC) insertion practice and reduces catheter failure in hospitalized adult patients. The main questions it aims to answer are: (1) Does the rate of PIVC failure decrease after the intervention compared with before? (2) Do nurses' PIVC practice, knowledge and self-regulated learning scores improve after the intervention? (3) How accurately do nurses assess their own practice, and how do they experience the process?

Catheter complications in two surgical wards were monitored for 12 weeks before the intervention. Nurses then performed PIVC insertion on a manikin while being video-recorded, watched their own video, scored themselves with a standardized checklist, compared their scores with the researcher's scores in a feedback session, and set personal improvement goals. Their practice was recorded again later in the 8-week intervention period. Catheter complications were monitored again for 12 weeks after the intervention. Nurses were also interviewed about their experience.
conditions: Extravasation of Diagnostic and Therapeutic Materials
title: Video-Assisted Self-Assessment and Feedback for Peripheral Intravenous Catheter Insertion

brief_summary:
Doctors often need to know how well a patient is breathing. Two things matter: how much air a person moves with each breath, and how hard the breathing muscles are working. Today, measuring these usually requires devices placed on or inside the body, which can be uncomfortable and are not always suitable at the bedside.

This study tests a new way to measure breathing without touching the body. A set of cameras films the surface of the chest and neck and builds a three-dimensional image of how they move during breathing. A computer uses these movements to estimate the amount of air breathed and to detect when the breathing muscles are being used.

The purpose of this study is to check whether the camera-based method is accurate. To do this, the researchers compare it with standard breathing measurements in healthy adult volunteers. During a single session, volunteers breathe normally and then breathe against increasing resistance, which makes breathing a little harder, while the cameras and the standard devices record at the same time.

The study will include 10 healthy volunteers (5 women and 5 men). It does not involve any treatment, and no results are expected to directly benefit the participants. If the method proves accurate, it could later be tested in patients to help monitor breathing in intensive care.
interventions: Three-dimensional markerless video system for respiratory surface motion analysis
primary_outcomes: Agreement between video-estimated and spirometry-measured tidal volume (bias)
title: 3D Video to Measure Breathing and Breathing-Muscle Activity

brief_summary:
Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) is a common operation for men with an enlarged prostate (benign prostatic hyperplasia) that blocks the flow of urine. Most men improve after surgery, but some remain bothered by urinary symptoms or are unsure whether the operation worked, and patients rarely see what was done during their operation.

This pilot randomized trial will find out whether a larger trial is feasible, and will take a first look at whether showing men their own before-and-after pictures of the prostate improves satisfaction with surgery. Fifty men having TURP at University Hospital, London, Ontario, will be randomly assigned after surgery to be shown their pre-TURP and post-resection images at each routine follow-up visit (6 weeks, 3 months and 6 months), or to usual follow-up.

The main outcomes are recruitment, retention, delivery of the image viewing, and completeness of data. Satisfaction, urinary symptoms and urine flow will be compared between groups as exploratory outcomes.
interventions: Viewing of own pre- and post-resection cystoscopic images
lead_sponsor: London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute OR Lawson Research Institute of St. Joseph's
title: Viewing Prostate Images After TURP: A Pilot Randomized Trial of Patient Satisfaction

brief_summary: This virtual, two-arm, randomized, triple-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluated whether daily supplementation with Oxxynea, a polyphenol-rich botanical blend, improves gastrointestinal comfort in adults using GLP-1-based therapies who experience gastrointestinal symptoms and report low fruit and vegetable intake. Participants took one capsule daily with the first meal of the day for six weeks and completed questionnaires at home.
primary_outcomes: Change in GIQLI Gastrointestinal Symptoms domain score
title: Oxxynea Supplementation for Gut Comfort in GLP-1-Based Therapy Users

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical study is to learn if the Ewing criteria work as a diagnostic and prognostic method for cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction in patients with spinal cord injury. It will also learn about specific cut-off points for these patients and the prognostic value of the tests for clinical events. The main questions it aims to answer are:

Is the Ewing battery applicable and valid for detecting cardiovascular dysautonomia in individuals with spinal cord injury? Do specific cut-off points improve the diagnostic accuracy of the Ewing tests for patients with spinal cord injury? Do the scores obtained by the Ewing tests present prognostic value for clinical autonomic events over a 12-month follow-up? Researchers will compare individuals with spinal cord injury to a healthy control group (adults with no previous comorbidities) to see if the Ewing criteria work to detect and classify dysautonomia.

Participants will:

Undergo the standardized Ewing battery of tests, including deep breathing, the Valsalva maneuver, and postural changes, in a controlled environment Have their heart rate and blood pressure monitored continuously and non-invasively during the execution of the tests Be followed for 12 months to record the occurrence and frequency of clinical events such as autonomic dysreflexia, symptomatic orthostatic hypotension, syncope, and hospitalizations
lead_sponsor: University of Sao Paulo General Hospital
primary_outcomes: Diagnostic Sensitivity and Specificity and Score Validation
Diagnostic Specificity of the Ewing Classification Tiers
title: Severity of Autonomic Dysfunction in Patients With Spinal Cord Injury: Evaluation and Validation of the Ewing Criteria for Assessing the Autonomic Nervous System in Spinal Cord Injury

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if E-WORTH South (Empowering African-American Women on the Road to Health - South), an adaptation of an evidence-based HIV prevention intervention, increases pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) use and reduces condomless sex among Black women at risk for HIV who are under non-carceral correctional supervision (probation, parole, or drug court) in Alabama. The main question it aims to answer is:

• Does E-WORTH South increase PrEP uptake and reduce condomless sex at 6 months compared with usual care?

Researchers will compare E-WORTH South with usual care to see if E-WORTH South increases PrEP uptake and reduces condomless sex. Participants will:

* Be randomly assigned to E-WORTH South or usual care
* In the E-WORTH South arm, attend five 90-minute sessions: one individual session within one week of enrollment, then four weekly group sessions on HIV prevention, safety, and trust, beginning after a 2- to 4-week group formation period
* In the usual care arm, receive one brief HIV prevention education session, HIV prevention counseling, referrals, and a directory of local services at enrollment
* Complete surveys and HIV and sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing at enrollment and at 3, 6, and 12 months
title: HIV Prevention for Women in Non-carceral Correctional Supervision Programs: A Hybrid Type II Trial of E-WORTH South

brief_summary:
This study examined whether temporary increases in upper-arm circumference immediately after resistance exercise were associated with changes in muscle thickness following 12 weeks of training.

Twenty-four healthy, resistance-trained men participated in a supervised exercise program three times per week. Upper-arm circumference was measured before and immediately after each weekly arm-training session. Biceps and triceps muscle thickness was assessed using ultrasound before the training program and 48 hours after the final session.

The study investigated whether individuals showing greater short-term increases in arm circumference also experienced greater changes in muscle thickness over the training period. Reported protein and energy intake were also considered in the analyses.
primary_outcomes: Change in Biceps Brachii Muscle Thickness
Change in Triceps Brachii Muscle Thickness
title: Acute Arm Circumference Responses and Muscle Growth After 12 Weeks of Resistance Training

brief_summary: This observational study aims to describe the clinical profile and outcomes of neonates admitted to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) at Sohag University Hospital, Egypt. The study will characterize the demographic and clinical features of admitted neonates, describe the main reasons for NICU admission, and assess their outcomes during hospitalization. The findings are expected to provide information about the characteristics and outcomes of neonates admitted to the unit.
title: Clinical Profile and Outcomes of NICU-Admitted Neonates at Sohag University Hospital

This randomized controlled trial aims to compare the effects of mobile app-guided versus supervised corrective exercise programs on pain intensity, postural alignment, and functional outcomes in patients with Text Neck Syndrome.
title: Comparative Effects of Mobile App-Guided Versus Supervised Corrective Exercise Programs in Patients With Text Neck Syndrome

It occurs due to inflammation in joint capsule. This study aim to determine the effect of motor control exercises versus conventional exercises in frozen shoulder.
title: Effects of Motor Control Exercises in Patients With Frozen Shoulder

brief_summary:
Low blood pressure following the induction of general anesthesia is a common complication, particularly in older adults. Propofol is widely used to induce general anesthesia; however, its administration may cause a significant decrease in blood pressure.

This study aims to determine whether a propofol self-co-induction technique, also known as propofol priming, can reduce the total dose of propofol required to induce general anesthesia compared with a standard induction technique. The study will also evaluate changes in blood pressure and heart rate, as well as adverse events during anesthetic induction.

This is a prospective, randomized, controlled, double-blind clinical trial conducted at Clínica Dávila in Santiago, Chile. The study will include adults aged 65 to 80 years undergoing elective surgery under general anesthesia with planned use of a laryngeal mask airway.

Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. The intervention group will receive an initial low dose of propofol before anesthetic induction, while the control group will receive a saline placebo. Both groups will subsequently receive propofol until loss of consciousness is achieved.

The primary outcome will be the total dose of propofol required for anesthetic induction. Secondary outcomes will include the occurrence of hypotension, changes in heart rate, and adverse events related to anesthetic induction.

primary_outcomes: Total Propofol Dose Required for Anesthetic Induction
title: Propofol Self-Co-Induction Versus Standard Induction in Older Adults Undergoing Elective Surgery

brief_summary:
Introduction Chronic Subacromial Pain Syndrome (CSAPS) is often characterized by alterations in pain modulation pathways, leading to a dissociation between pain intensity and the actual degree of tissue damage in the shoulder. The impact of chronic pain can be categorized into peripheral sensitization and changes in central pain modulation pathways. Common peripheral phenomena include an increase in active and latent myofascial trigger points (MTrPs) and a decreased pressure pain threshold (PPT). Central modulation changes involve dysfunctional descending inhibitory pathways due to weakened GABAergic inhibition, or increased ascending pathway excitability caused by persistent C-fiber activation of dorsal horn neurons and subsequent glutamate release. Previous literature has established that the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and primary motor cortex (M1) are interconnected and can simultaneously process nociceptive stimuli. Consequently, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is frequently utilized in chronic pain research to investigate intracortical facilitation within ascending pathways and intracortical inhibition within descending pathways. This approach effectively reveals the alterations in ascending and descending pain modulatory pathways associated with chronic pain. However, the underlying mechanisms by which myofascial trigger points (MTrPs) therapy influences these pain modulatory pathways remain unclear, underscoring the need for further investigation.

Purpose This study aims to investigate changes in motor cortex parameters following MTrP therapy in patients with CSAPS to explore its impact on pain modulation pathways. Additionally, the study examines whether the combination of MTrP therapy and exercise training is superior to exercise training alone in improving pain, function, and pain modulation.

Method A randomized controlled trial will be conducted, recruiting a total of 40 participants (accounting for a 20% attrition rate). Eligible participants will be aged 18-65, diagnosed with CSAPS for over three months, and present with active or latent MTrPs. Inclusion criteria include a maximum Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS) score greater than 3 and fulfillment of specific subacromial pain syndrome diagnostic criteria. Participants will be randomly assigned to two groups (n=20 per group): MTrP therapy plus shoulder exercise (intervention group) or shoulder exercise alone (control group). Both groups will receive interventions twice weekly for four weeks. The primary outcome measures are TMS-derived cortical excitability and inhibitory indices, including Resting Motor Threshold (RMT), Active Motor Threshold (AMT), Motor Evoked Potential (MEP), Cortical Silent Period (CSP), Short-Interval Intracortical Inhibition (SICI), Long-Interval Intracortical Inhibition (LICI), Intracortical Facilitation (ICF), and Short-Interval Intracortical Facilitation (SICF).

Secondary outcomes include the Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH), score, pain scales, depression scales, and bilateral PPT measured at three specific sites.

Statistical Analysis Baseline characteristics will be analyzed using descriptive statistics. Categorical data will be assessed using the Chi-square test. Continuous data will be evaluated for normality using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Between-group differences in continuous data will be analyzed using the independent t-test for normally distributed data or the Mann-Whitney U test for non-normally distributed data.
lead_sponsor: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
primary_outcomes: Active Motor Threshold (AMT) Measured by Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation
Short-Interval Intracortical Inhibition (SICI) as Measured by Paired-Pulse Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation
Intracortical Facilitation (ICF) as Measured by Paired-Pulse Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation
Long-Interval Intracortical Inhibition (LICI) as Measured by Paired-Pulse Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation
Short-Interval Intracortical Facilitation (SICF) as Measured by Paired-Pulse Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation
title: Combined Trigger Point Therapy and Exercise on Pain Regulation Pathways in Chronic Subacromial Pain Syndrome

This study will evaluate the safety of this treatment approach and assess changes in prostate size, urinary symptoms, erectile function, and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels. The study will also evaluate whether PAE may help some patients become eligible for stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) by reducing prostate size or improving urinary symptoms.

brief_summary: Childhood obesity can negatively affect balance, coordination, mobility, and dual-task performance. This study aims to evaluate the effects of Standardized Walking Obstacle Course (SWOC) activities on dual-task performance in obese children aged 4-12 years. A randomized controlled trial will compare an experimental group receiving SWOC training three times weekly for 12 weeks with a control group receiving strengthening exercises. Outcomes will include dual-task performance, gait speed, and dual-task cost, analyzed using SPSS version 26, with significance set at p \< 0.05.
title: Effects of Standarized Walking Obstacle Course on Task Performance in Children

brief_summary: Introduction Vanishing Lung Syndrome (VLS) is a severe form of bullous lung disease characterized by giant emphysematous bullae compressing functional lung parenchyma. Surgical resection via open thoracotomy remains a key intervention in symptomatic or complicated cases. However, persistent postoperative air leaks remain a major challenge, contributing to prolonged chest tube duration, extended hospitalization, and increased morbidity. This prospective study compares outcomes among patients undergoing open bullectomy with no reinforcement, synthetic mesh reinforcement, and autologous fat patch reinforcement of the staple line.
title: Prolonged Air Leaks in Lung Surgery for Vanishing Lung Syndrome

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn whether vitamin D, zinc, or both, taken in addition to usual care for 12 weeks, reduce symptom severity in adults with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Does vitamin D lower the IBS Symptom Severity Score (IBS-SSS) at week 12 compared with usual care alone?
* Does zinc lower the IBS-SSS at week 12 compared with usual care alone?
* Does the IBS-SSS at week 12 differ between vitamin D and zinc? Researchers will compare four groups: vitamin D3, zinc, vitamin D3 plus zinc, and usual care alone.

Participants will:

* Have blood tests for vitamin D and zinc at the start and at week 12
* Take their assigned supplement(s) for 12 weeks, in addition to their usual IBS treatment
* Visit the clinic at the start and at week 12, and complete IBS symptom and quality-of-life questionnaires
title: Vitamin D Versus Zinc Supplementation for Symptom Severity in Irritable Bowel Syndrome

brief_summary:
This study aims to evaluate the effect of local cold application on pain and vital signs in adult patients undergoing thyroid fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB).

The study is a randomized controlled trial involving 100 participants divided into two groups: an intervention group (n=50) and a control group (n=50). Participants in the intervention group receive local cold application using an ice pack for 15 minutes before and 15 minutes after the biopsy. Participants in the control group receive routine care without the additional cold application.

Pain is assessed using the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) before, during, and after the biopsy. The Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire is administered 15 minutes after the procedure. Vital signs are also assessed to evaluate physiological responses. The study aims to determine whether local cold application can provide a simple, non-pharmacological approach to pain management in patients undergoing thyroid FNAB.
primary_outcomes: Pain Intensity Before Thyroid Fine-Needle Aspiration Biopsy
Pain Intensity After Thyroid Fine-Needle Aspiration Biopsy
Pain Assessment Using the Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire
Pain Intensity During Thyroid Fine-Needle Aspiration Biopsy
title: Effect of Local Cold Application on Pain and Vital Signs During Thyroid Fine-Needle Aspiration Biopsy

brief_summary: This pilot study tested whether people with chronic stroke can learn to control a virtual cursor through the activity of their shoulder and elbow muscles (EMG control) as well as they control it through the force they generate (force control). Six people with chronic stroke performed an isometric virtual reaching task with the paretic arm in 12 sessions over four weeks. In each session, cursor motion was driven either by the force measured at the hand or by the force estimated from multi-muscle EMG through a participant-specific EMG-to-force mapping. Performance in the two control modalities was compared across sessions, together with upper-limb motor function and muscle synergies. The study corresponds to Aim 2 of project GR-2019-12370271 and precedes the randomized trial of assistive myoelectric control registered as NCT06911671 (ERICA).
lead_sponsor: LIFE - Research and Care Institute - Santa Lucia IRCCS
primary_outcomes: Feasibility of EMG control: initial direction error of the cursor in EMG control relative to force control
title: Learning Myoelectric Control of an Isometric Virtual Reaching Task After Stroke: a 12-Session Pilot Study

brief_summary:
This pilot feasibility study evaluated the safety, feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary functional outcomes of an 8-week community-based Taekwondo (TKD) exercise program for older adults and individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD).

Using a single-group, repeated-measures design, 14 community-dwelling adults (10 older adults without PD and 4 individuals with mild-to-moderate PD) participated in instructor-led Taekwondo classes twice weekly for eight weeks (16 sessions, 50 minutes each). The program incorporated adapted Taekwondo movements, including stepping, kicking, punching, choreographed movement sequences (poomsae), and balance and coordination exercises.

Participants completed assessments at two baseline timepoints, immediately after the intervention, and at a six-month follow-up. Outcomes included balance, gait speed, functional mobility, walking endurance, cognitive function, balance confidence, and postural sway. Program feasibility and safety were evaluated through attendance records and adverse event monitoring, while participant experiences and acceptability were explored through semi-structured interviews.

The study aimed to establish the feasibility of community-based Taekwondo training and generate preliminary evidence to inform future clinical trials involving older adults and individuals with Parkinson's disease.
lead_sponsor: State University of New York - Upstate Medical University
primary_outcomes: Number of Participants Experiencing Intervention-Related Serious Adverse Events
title: Feasibility and Optimization of a Community-Based Mind-Body Taekwondo Intervention for Parkinson's Disease.

brief_summary:
The goal of this observational study is to learn whether blood levels of soluble tumor necrosis factor receptor 1 (sTNFR-1), a protein related to inflammation, can help predict long-term kidney problems in adults who have severe acute kidney injury, a sudden, major decline in kidney function.

The main questions this study aims to answer are:

* How often do patients develop chronic kidney disease, experience worsening of existing kidney disease, or develop kidney failure within 12 months after severe acute kidney injury?
* Can sTNFR-1 levels help predict these kidney outcomes?
* Can sTNFR-1 levels help predict death, continued need for dialysis or other kidney replacement therapy, or a substantial decline in kidney function? The study plans to enroll at least 196 adults aged 18 years or older with severe acute kidney injury at Nhan Dan Gia Dinh Hospital in Vietnam.

Participants will:

* Have blood collected to measure sTNFR-1 within 24 hours after severe acute kidney injury is identified and again at 3 months.
* Be monitored during hospitalization and assessed at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months after discharge.
* Have blood and urine tests to assess kidney function and provide information about dialysis, hospital readmissions, and other health events.

Researchers will examine whether sTNFR-1 levels improve the prediction of kidney outcomes when added to an existing clinical risk model. Participants will receive medical care from their treating clinicians without treatment assignment by the study.
primary_outcomes: Predictive Performance of sTNFR-1 for New-Onset or Progressive Chronic Kidney Disease or Kidney Failure.
title: Predictive Value of sTNFR-1 Levels for Chronic Kidney Disease Progression After Severe Acute Kidney Injury

brief_summary: This study will compare two procedures for knee pain caused by osteoarthritis. One procedure blocks small arteries supplying the painful area of the knee. The other uses cold to treat nerves that carry pain signals from the knee. Each eligible knee will be assigned by chance to one of the procedures. The main question is how much pain, stiffness, and difficulty with daily activities improve six months after the first technically successful procedure. Participants will also report knee symptoms and function at three and twelve months. If symptoms improve by less than the study threshold at six months, the study team will offer the other procedure when clinically appropriate.
primary_outcomes: Improvement in the normalized WOMAC total score at six months
title: Artery Embolization Versus Nerve Cryoablation for Knee Osteoarthritis

brief_summary:
Obesity is a condition where a person has excessive body fat, defined by a body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m2 or higher. The goal of this study is to evaluate the effect of various doses of ABBV-295 compared to placebo on reducing body weight at Week 32 in participants with obesity or overweight with weight-related comorbidities.

ABBV-295 is an investigational medicine being developed to help manage body weight over time. This study is double-blind, which means that neither the participants nor the study doctors know who is given which study treatment. At the start of the study, participants will be randomized to 1 of 6 groups that will receive different doses. and/dosing schedules of ABBV-295 or placebo. For every 5 patients who receive ABBV-295, one patient will receive placebo. This study will include approximately 360 patients between the ages of 18 and 75 years with a body mass index (BMI) of at least 27.0 at approximately 70 sites across the world.

ABBV-295 and placebo will be given as an injection under the skin. Participants will receive study treatment for 52 weeks.

There may be a bigger responsibility for participants in this study compared to patients who receive standard of care treatment. Participants will attend regular visits during the study at a hospital or clinic. The effects of treatment will be checked by medical assessments, blood tests, checking for side effects, and completing questionnaires.
primary_outcomes: Percent Change From Baseline in Body Weight
title: Study of Subcutaneous ABBV-295 to Assess Adverse Events and Change in Disease Activity in Adults With Obesity or Overweight

brief_summary: The goal of this preliminary study, being conducted preparatory to future research, is to evaluate the sensitivity of a torque cell device to measure finger extensor strength combined with a motorized lever that forces the fingers through an arc of approximately 60 degrees (from extended to flexed) in detection of McArdle sign. McArdle sign is a specific sign of multiple sclerosis wherein muscles, in particular finger extensors, become transiently weaker with neck flexion compared to neck extension; the PI previously studied and published on this phenomenon with a similar first generation device without a motorized lever and now wishes to evaluate the new device compared to clinical assessment in patients with MS, stratified according to degree of baseline weakness and clinical degree of McArdle sign. The investigators don't plan to publish the data from this study directly, but plan to retain the data from this study and combine with additional data to be collected in future studies to be submitted to the IRB-HSR to further the general goals of the program: to understand the phenomenon of McArdle sign and its application to diagnosis, predicting response to treatment, serving as outcome measure in patients with MS.
primary_outcomes: Change in finger extensor strength with neck flexion compared to neck extension
title: McArdle Sign Study

brief_summary:
The goal of this randomized controlled trial is to investigate whether a six-week online mindfulness-based intervention can reduce depressive symptoms and improve mental health and psychological well-being in adults with morning or evening chronotypes.

Chronotype refers to individual differences in preferred timing of sleep, activity, and alertness. Individuals with morning chronotypes tend to feel more alert and energetic earlier in the day, whereas those with evening chronotypes tend to prefer later hours. Evening chronotypes may be more vulnerable to certain mental health difficulties, including depressive symptoms, anxiety, and sleep problems. Mindfulness-based interventions aim to develop present-moment awareness and a more accepting, nonjudgmental relationship with thoughts, emotions, and bodily sensations.

The main research questions are:

1. Does a six-week online mindfulness-based intervention reduce depressive symptoms compared with a waitlist control condition?
2. Does the effectiveness of the intervention differ between individuals with morning and evening chronotypes?
3. Does the intervention improve anxiety symptoms, psychological well-being, perceived stress, sleep disturbances, and psychological processes including mindfulness, self-compassion, cognitive fusion, and repetitive negative thinking?
4. Do changes in psychological processes, particularly mindfulness, cognitive fusion, and repetitive negative thinking, help explain improvements in depressive symptoms?
5. Are improvements maintained one month and three months after the intervention?

Approximately 400 adults with pronounced morning or evening chronotypes will be enrolled and randomly assigned to one of two groups, with randomization stratified by chronotype:

1. Mindfulness intervention group: Participants will complete a six-week online mindfulness-based program adapted from Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT). The intervention will include one live, instructor-led online group session per week, lasting approximately 60-120 minutes, and guided individual mindfulness practice lasting approximately 20-30 minutes per day, six days per week. Guided practice materials will be provided through the study's online platform. The platform will also be used to monitor engagement with the intervention, including access to guided meditation recordings and practice duration.
2. Control group: Participants will not receive mindfulness training during the six-week intervention period. After the mindfulness intervention group completes the six-week program, participants in the waitlist control group will be given access to an asynchronous, self-guided version of the mindfulness training.

Participants will complete standardized questionnaires assessing depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, psychological well-being, sleep difficulties, perceived stress, and psychological processes potentially involved in the effects of mindfulness training.

The primary outcome will be depressive symptom severity, assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-8 (PHQ-8). Secondary outcomes will include anxiety symptoms assessed using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), psychological well-being assessed using the World Health Organization-Five Well-Being Index (WHO-5), sleep disturbances assessed using the PROMIS Sleep Disturbance Short Form 6a (PROMIS SD SF-6a), and perceived stress assessed using the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10). The study will also assess changes in dispositional mindfulness (FFMQ-15), repetitive negative thinking (PTQ-15), cognitive fusion (CFQ-7), and self-compassion (SCS-SF). These measures will allow to investigate potential psychological mechanisms underlying the effects of mindfulness training, including whether earlier changes in mindfulness and cognitive fusion are associated with subsequent reductions in repetitive negative thinking and depressive symptoms.

Questionnaire assessments will be conducted before the intervention (Week 0), during the intervention (Weeks 2 and 4), and immediately after the intervention (Week 6). Additional follow-up assessments will take place one month and three months after the intervention to examine the maintenance of treatment effects.

The findings may contribute to a better understanding of whether mindfulness-based interventions are similarly effective for individuals with morning and evening chronotypes, how mindfulness-related psychological processes change during treatment, and whether chronotype should be considered when developing accessible online mental health interventions.
title: Mindfulness-Based Intervention and Mental Health Outcomes in Morning and Evening Chronotypes

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if body identical hormone therapy estradiol and progesterone (approved by the FDA) reduces risk of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias, heart disease, and loss of brain function in healthy women who have been post-menopausal for less than 6 years and are currently 45-59 years old. The main questions we aim to answer are:

In women less than 6 years from menopause without dementia and heart disease, does hormone therapy decrease

* Alzheimer's disease brain markers measured by brain MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)?
* heart disease markers measured by ultrasound of arteries?
* decline in age-related memory, thinking, and other brain functions?
primary_outcomes: Longitudinal change in MRI-based measurement of cerebrovascular reactivity (CVR)
title: Alzheimer's Risk Intervention Trial With Estradiol

brief_summary:
This study looks at three ways to help manage pain without medication: virtual reality (using a VR headset to create an immersive distraction), hypnosis (using guided relaxation and suggestion), and a combination of both. Researchers want to know which approach - or combination - works best at reducing pain and discomfort.

Forty healthy adults will take part in a single research visit lasting about 140 minutes. During the visit, participants will experience mild, controlled pain from a small electrical stimulation on the ankle, adjusted to a level they can tolerate. They will try all three approaches (virtual reality, hypnosis, and the combination) during the same visit, in a random order. Throughout the visit, researchers will record how much pain and discomfort participants feel, along with body signals such as heart rate, breathing, skin response, and brain activity (using a comfortable EEG cap with no needles).

The goal is to better understand how these non-drug approaches work and whether combining them provides more relief than using either one alone. This research may help improve pain management for people undergoing medical procedures in the future.
lead_sponsor: Ciusss de L'Est de l'Île de Montréal
title: Comparing Virtual Reality, Hypnosis, and Their Combination for Experimental Pain Modulation

brief_summary: The study will use a randomized clinical trial design to investigate the effects of short foot exercises with and without proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF) in school-going children with pes planus. The study will be conducted at schools and will include 76 participants randomly allocated into two equal groups. One group will receive short foot exercises, while the other will receive short foot exercises combined with PNF techniques. Pre- and post-intervention assessments will be conducted to compare changes in foot posture, balance, and functional performance. Data will be analyzed using SPSS version 26.0.
title: Effects of Short Foot Exercises With and Without PNF on School Going Children With Pes Planus

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn whether trained pharmacists can use the Penicillin Allergy Decision Rule (PEN-FAST) clinical decision rule to assess penicillin allergy risk similarly to physicians in adults who are hospitalized and have a penicillin allergy recorded in their medical record.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Among participants assessed as having a low risk of penicillin allergy, is the proportion who proceed with an amoxicillin challenge similar between those assessed by pharmacists and those assessed by physicians?
* Among participants who undergo an amoxicillin challenge, how many develop an allergic reaction within 1 hour of taking amoxicillin?

Researchers will compare pharmacist-led PEN-FAST assessment with physician-led PEN-FAST assessment. Both groups will use the same eligibility criteria, safety procedures, counselling process, and pathways for medical review.

Participants will:

* Have their penicillin allergy history assessed using the PEN-FAST clinical decision rule by either a trained pharmacist or physician.
* Complete questionnaires about their penicillin allergy, concerns, and quality of life.
* Be offered an oral amoxicillin challenge if they are assessed as having a low risk of penicillin allergy and are suitable to proceed. The challenge is optional and may be done during the hospital admission or later in the outpatient setting.
* Be assessed for immediate allergic reactions during the amoxicillin challenge, including reactions occurring within 1 hour after taking amoxicillin.
* Be assessed again about 3 to 5 days after the challenge for delayed allergic reactions.
* Have information from their medical records reviewed for up to 24 months after the PEN-FAST assessment.

The study will also look at the range of PEN-FAST risk scores, reasons why eligible participants do not proceed with amoxicillin challenge, immediate and delayed allergic reactions, participant perceptions and quality of life, antibiotic use, infection-related outcomes, hospital stay, and other healthcare use.
title: Pharmacist Versus Physician PEN-FAST Assessment in Hospitalised Adults With a Penicillin Allergy Label

brief_summary:
This study tests whether artificial intelligence messages to clinicians improve the use of recommended medicines in adults with diabetes and chronic kidney disease. The tool reviews existing medical records and places patient-specific recommendations in internal Epic Huddle notes before endocrinology or cardiology visits at Mass General Brigham.

Eligible visits during approximately 3-6 months before implementation are compared with visits during approximately 3-6 months afterward among the same clinicians, without randomization. Outcomes include medication optimization within 30 days, message delivery, and short-term safety. Patients are not contacted, and all treatment decisions remain with clinicians and patients.
conditions: Chronic Kidney Disease Due to Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
interventions: LLM CKD GDMT Clinical Decision Support
primary_outcomes: Any GDMT optimization within 30 days of the index visit
title: Targeted Artificial Intelligence Language mOdel Recommendations for Chronic Kidney Disease

brief_summary: This is an experimental single-arm, open-label, interventional pilot feasibility study designed to evaluate the safety, feasibility, and biologic impact of pulsed electric field (PEF) ablation administered during the CAR T-cell vein-to-vein interval. We will enroll 5 subjects in this pilot trial. The primary objective is to understand the feasibility of the intervention in the proposed study population. We will measure this by Calculation of the percentage of subjects who receive PEF ablation and successfully receive a CAR T-cell infusion. The secondary objectives include metabolic tumor volume dynamics, CAR-T expansion and persistence via CareDx, cytokine/immune profiling across key timepoints, and spatial (abscopal) response of treated vs untreated lesions. These will be measured in the days following PEF ablation with IRE and CAR-T infusion, up to 6 months following CAR-T infusion.
primary_outcomes: The percentage of subjects who receive PEF ablation and successfully receive a CAR T-cell infusion.
title: A Pilot Feasibility Study of Pulsed Electric Field (PEF) Tumor Priming Before Lisocabtagene Maraleucel (Liso-cel) in Relapsed/Refractory B-cell Malignancies

brief_summary:
Previous experimental studies have demonstrated that intravenous administration of MaxiPost, a large-conductance calcium-activated potassium (BKCa) channel opener, can induce migraine attacks in people with migraine without aura. However, whether BKCa channel opening can induce migraine aura remains unknown.

This randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-period crossover study aims to determine whether intravenous MaxiPost induces migraine attacks with aura in people with migraine with aura.
primary_outcomes: Incidence of migraine attacks with aura
title: Induction of Migraine Attacks With Aura and Opening of BKCa Channels

brief_summary:
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder in children, characterized by inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity. Pharmacological treatment plays an important role in managing ADHD symptoms and improving daily functioning.

Methylphenidate, a stimulant medication, and atomoxetine, a non-stimulant medication, are commonly used for the treatment of ADHD in children. Although both medications have demonstrated efficacy, their comparative effectiveness and safety may vary among children.

This randomized controlled trial was conducted to compare the efficacy and safety of methylphenidate and atomoxetine in children aged 6-12 years diagnosed with ADHD according to DSM-5 criteria.

A total of 120 eligible children were randomly allocated into two groups. Group A received methylphenidate, while Group B received atomoxetine. Medication was initiated at recommended starting doses and adjusted gradually according to clinical response and tolerability. Both groups also received behavioural therapy consisting of one 40-minute session per week in the hospital.

Participants were followed for six months, with assessments conducted at baseline, two weeks, one and a half months, three months and six months. ADHD symptoms were assessed using the SNAP-IV Parent Rating Scale during follow-up and the Conners ADHD Index at baseline and six months. The primary efficacy assessment was the change in Conners ADHD Index T-score from baseline to six months.

Safety assessments included monitoring of weight, height, pulse, blood pressure and two most common medication-related adverse effects; decreased appetite, sleep difficulties.

The study provided a comparison of the effectiveness and tolerability of methylphenidate and atomoxetine in children with ADHD and contributed local clinical evidence to plan pharmacological treatment decisions.
lead_sponsor: Children's Hospital and Institute of Child Health, Multan
primary_outcomes: Change in Conners ADHD Index T-score from baseline to 6 months.
title: Comparison of Methylphenidate and Atomoxetine for the Treatment of ADHD in Children Aged 6 to 12 Years

brief_summary: The aim of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of apically positioned flap (APF) surgery in increasing buccal tissue thickness around dental implants and to compare the diagnostic reliability of ultrasonography with traditional transgingival probing for monitoring postoperative tissue changes.
primary_outcomes: Diagnostic Concordance Between Ultrasonography and Transgingival Probing
title: Ultrasound and Probing of Peri-Implant Soft Tissue After Apically Positioned Flap

brief_summary:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common heart rhythm disorder. Catheter ablation, a minimally invasive procedure that treats small areas of heart tissue to block abnormal electrical signals, is a standard treatment. In people whose AF has been continuous for a long time and whose left atrium is enlarged ("advanced persistent AF"), standard ablation works in only about half of patients.

The purpose of this study is to find out whether a more extensive ablation strategy, modeled on the surgical Cox-Maze operation but performed through catheters, controls abnormal atrial rhythms better than the standard strategy.

One hundred adults with advanced persistent AF who are having their first ablation will be assigned by chance to one of two groups. The standard group will receive isolation of the pulmonary veins and of the back wall of the left atrium. The Maze-like group will receive the same treatment plus additional ablation lines in both the left and right atria. All procedures use the same ablation system.

A small heart monitor will be placed under the skin of every participant to record heart rhythm continuously for 12 months. The main comparison is the amount of time participants spend in abnormal atrial rhythms, together with the need for a repeat ablation or for new or increased rhythm-control medication, between 2 and 12 months after the procedure.
title: A Randomized Controlled Trial of a Percutaneous Maze-like Catheter Ablation Strategy for Advanced Persistent Atrial Fibrillation

brief_summary: Movement and physical activity play a vital role in the development of the brain, motor coordination and cognitive abilities in childhood. In many schools, structured physical activity is often neglected because of academic pressures and limited time to complete school curriculum. As a result, school children fail to meet the recommended physical activity levels, which may negatively affect their physical fitness, endurance and executive functioning. Recent evidence suggests that integrating movement-based activities with cognitive demands, such as auditory motor sequencing games, can enhance both motor performance and higher-order cognitive skills in young children. This study aims to investigate the effects of auditory motor sequencing games on endurance and executive functions in school going children.
title: Effects of Auditory Motor Sequencing Games on Endurance and Executive Functions in School Going Children

brief_summary: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the impact of glucose visibility provided by the Stelo Glucose Biosensor System on participants' glucose insight, decision confidence, self-regulation, and health-related behaviors. The study enrolls US-based adults (≥18 years) across four groups: individuals with type 2 diabetes not treated with insulin, individuals with prediabetes, individuals in perimenopause, and healthy-living individuals. Participants complete baseline assessments and a blinded Stelo wear period, followed by \~30 days of unblinded Stelo use across two consecutive wear periods. Behavioral, psychosocial, and glycemic outcomes are assessed through periodic patient-reported outcome (PRO) surveys and semi-structured interviews collected at baseline, 15 days, and 30 days. The primary outcome is change in perceived glucose insight and decision confidence.
primary_outcomes: Change in participant-reported understanding of how food choices affect glucose
Change in participant-reported understanding of how physical activity affects glucose
Change in participant confidence in interpreting glucose trends and patterns
Change in participant confidence in making health-related decisions using glucose data
title: Stelo SPARK Study: Behavioral and Glycemic Effects of Glucose Visibility

brief_summary: This study will evaluate the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of KR25102 Tablets in healthy adult participants. KR25102 is an investigational drug being developed to treat acute pain by targeting a specific sodium channel (Na1.8) in the peripheral nervous system, potentially avoiding the side effects of opioids. The study is a single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-ascending-dose study. Approximately 33 healthy adults will be enrolled and randomized to one of four dose groups (20 mg, 40 mg, 80 mg, or 120 mg) or a placebo. Participants will receive a single oral dose of the study drug under fasting conditions, followed by an 8-day in-patient observation period and a follow-up period.
interventions: Single Ascending Dose of KR25102 Tablets
lead_sponsor: The Third Xiangya Hospital of Central South University

Number of Participants with Serious Adverse Events
Number of Participants with Adverse Events Leading to Discontinuation of Study Drug

Number of Participants with Clinically Significant Abnormalities on Physical Examination
Number of Participants with Clinically Significant Abnormalities on 12-Lead Electrocardiogram
